content: The World Health Organization (WHO) and its partners developed updated diagnostic algorithms for tuberculosis (TB), which were scheduled for release in 2020. These guidelines address concerns about the potential loss of global and national capacity for culture testing, which remains the current reference standard for identifying active TB disease. In studies evaluating the Xpert Ultra diagnostic test, a trace result was considered negative. However, Xpert Ultra is expected to produce more false-positive results for pulmonary TB compared to its predecessor, Xpert MTB/RIF. The recommendations for Xpert Ultra are limited to its use in clinical case management. When Xpert Ultra yields a positive result, clinical management should follow national guidelines. Conversely, if the result is negative, the patient should undergo clinical re-evaluation. For culture-positive results, clinical management should also adhere to national guidelines, while culture-negative results necessitate further clinical evaluation, potentially involving additional diagnostic tests. The Xpert MTB/RIF test is an automated molecular diagnostic tool that uses the GeneXpert platform. It can detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) bacteria and rifampicin resistance within two hours, requiring minimal hands-on technical time. Unlike conventional nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), the Xpert MTB/RIF integrates PCR amplification and detection into a single, self-contained cartridge. This design minimizes biosafety concerns during testing and allows the technology to be used closer to patients, outside of central or reference laboratories. However, the system requires a stable electrical power supply, temperature control, and annual calibration of its modules. Xpert Ultra, developed as a next-generation assay by Cepheid, addresses limitations in sensitivity for TB diagnosis. It incorporates two multicopy amplification targets (IS6110 and IS1081) and features a larger DNA reaction chamber (50 µL compared to 25 µL in Xpert MTB/RIF). Additionally, Xpert Ultra employs fully nested nucleic acid amplification, faster thermal cycling, and improved fluidics and enzymes. These enhancements result in a lower limit of detection (16 colony-forming units per milliliter, compared to 114 cfu/mL for Xpert MTB/RIF). For rifampicin resistance detection, Xpert Ultra uses melting-temperature-based analysis with four probes to identify mutations in the rifampicin-resistance-determining region of the rpoB gene. The WHO Global TB Programme initiated a systematic review to update its guidelines on the use of Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra for diagnosing TB in individuals with signs and symptoms of the disease. The review followed the Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome (PICO) framework to assess evidence and inform recommendations. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, which categorizes evidence quality as high, moderate, low, or very low. Diagnostic accuracy studies, even if observational, were initially rated as high-quality evidence. Quality assessments were independently conducted by at least two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Meta-analyses were performed to estimate pooled sensitivity and specificity for Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra, separately for pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance. For pulmonary TB detection, 94 studies were identified, including 85 evaluating Xpert MTB/RIF and nine evaluating both Xpert Ultra and Xpert MTB/RIF. Most studies were conducted in high TB burden and high TB/HIV burden countries, with low risk of bias and high applicability to primary care and local hospital settings. For rifampicin resistance detection, 57 studies evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF, with 27 conducted in high multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) burden countries. Most studies demonstrated low risk of bias. Xpert Ultra was evaluated in nine studies for pulmonary TB detection and eight studies for rifampicin resistance detection. The assay demonstrated high certainty of evidence in most studies. The systematic reviews aimed to summarize the diagnostic accuracy of Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra for TB and rifampicin resistance, contributing to the development of updated WHO guidelines for molecular assays as initial tests for TB diagnosis in adults and children.
